newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Fixing WHSmith will be long haul.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Fixing WHSmith will be long haul.

text.p: W.H. Smith Group Plc said on Wednesday its reorganisation over the past year was a step in the right direction, but improving the core W.H. Smith retail chain would be a long haul.
Chief executive Bill Cockburn said the reorganisation had created a springboard for the next phase which would aim to carry through the benefits and grow the top line.
He told Reuters in an interview after its half-year results the main retail chain was now the top priority for action.
"It's very important that we get that fixed and that's going to be a long haul, but we'll have benefits along the way."
Cockburn, who took the helm just a year ago, said new management at the retail chain had to capitalise on the strengths of its well-known high-street brand name.
He said 7.5 million shoppers visited the shops every week, but the key was to persuade them to spend and persuade those who did spend to spend more.

The stores held on to the top slots in market share in books, video, music, magazines, stationery and childrens "back to school" equipment. "Of course competition is building up, but we're holding our market shares in the key areas pretty well," the chief executive said.
Management had been vigorous in ridding the stores of unprofitable "clutter" and freeing up space for more profitable use.
Smiths will extend its new childrens' discovery range, trialled in 12 stores, into its larger shops. The group also plans to sell CDs and tapes in 90 of its smaller stores after a successful trial.
Cost reductions produced savings of nine million stg in the first half, with 14 million expected for the full year.
Cockburn said clearly there was the opportunity to go further. "There's always scope for improving efficiency and productivity."

He said boosting sales growth in the core chain was a top priority, but did not want to buy sales by diluting gross margin. "I don't think there's any mileage in buying sales by just discounting to uneconomic levels," he said. "What we've got to do is get that right balance between promotion, customer stimulation, but keeping your eye on your margins and growing the bottom line."
Gross margins improved by about one percentage point in the retail businesses in the first half, he said.
Cockburn said sales, including Christmas and into the new year, had been encouraging considering the upheaval caused by the reorganisation.
In the first half total like-for-like sales for the group rose by two percent, and by three percent in December. W.H. Sales at the Smith chain rose 1.5 percent in the first half.
Cockburn said sales since December had continued at the same sort of level.

He saw a big opportunity for expanding the group's hotel and airport store business in the United States, pointing out there were 60 airports in the country that would lend themselves to Smith's concept.

W.H. Smith held its dividend at 5.25 pence, but said it expected to introduce a progressive dividend policy as its financial performance improved. Cockburn said the group aimed to move closer to dividend cover of two times.

When asked about recent speculation in the press about a bid for W.H. Smith, Cockburn said, "We are the biggest seller of fiction in the country and sometimes we read fiction in the newspapers as well." -- Jane Merriman, London Newsroom + 44 171 542 7717
